# The one wire that made depth work

Two networks. **Twenty-six convolutions each, the same layers in the same order, trained on
the same data with the same seed.** The only difference is a single switch on every block:
`skip`, which either adds the block's input back onto its output or does not.

That addition is the whole of the 2015 ResNet paper, and it is why networks went from about
twenty layers deep to hundreds.

Note which model has *more* parameters. The plain stack has **366,938**; the residual one
has **369,690**. The extra 2,752 are two 1×1 projections, needed where the channel count
changes so that the two sides of the addition are the same shape. The better model is not
the bigger one — it is bigger *because* it is the better one.

## What is actually being claimed, and at what depth

The gap is not a constant. It is a function of depth, and at shallow depths it is nearly
nothing — which is why a demonstration at twelve layers proves the wrong thing.

| convolutions | residual | plain | gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14 | 0.6150 | 0.5945 | +0.021 |
| 20 | 0.5945 | 0.5680 | +0.027 |
| **26** | **0.5950** | **0.4760** | **+0.119** |
| 32 | 0.5920 | 0.4660 | +0.126 |

Read down the two middle columns rather than across. **The residual network barely moves**
— 0.615, 0.595, 0.595, 0.592 — it neither gains from depth nor suffers from it. **The plain
network falls off a cliff** between 20 and 26 layers: 0.595, 0.568, 0.476, 0.466.

That is the degradation problem, and it is not overfitting: the plain network is worse on
*training* data too. Extra layers make the thing harder to optimise, and the shortcut is
what removes the difficulty.

26 layers is used here because it is the shallowest depth where the effect is unmistakable
and the run still finishes in a few minutes.

**Do not expect to reproduce those exact numbers.** The table averages two seeds; a single
run of this workflow lands nearer 0.557 against 0.458. The absolute values move by several
points from the seed alone, and two seeds is not enough to say by how much. **The gap is the
reproducible part** — +0.10 to +0.12 here, and about +0.02 at 14 layers — which is why it is
the gap that the argument rests on and not the accuracies.

## Squeeze-and-excitation, and an honest null result

The third idea on this canvas is **channel attention**: pool each feature map to one number,
push those through a tiny two-layer bottleneck, and multiply every map by the resulting gate.
The network decides how loud each of its own channels should be.

It is elegant, it is two `Linear` layers, and **on this problem it does nothing.** Measured
at 14 convolutions: 0.6085 with it against 0.6150 without, for 5,656 extra parameters. The
difference is inside the seed spread, and the sign is the wrong way round.

That is not a claim that squeeze-and-excitation is useless — it earns its place on ImageNet
at far greater width. It is a claim that **it does not pay here**, and a workflow that
quietly omitted the measurement would be implying otherwise.

Wire the SE branch in below the residual stack if you want to re-run it.
